content: This document is an updated review of techniques used for female sterilization, originally published in 2002. Female sterilization is the most widely used contraceptive method globally. Various techniques are employed to interrupt the patency of the fallopian tubes, including cutting and tying the tubes, using electric current to damage the tubes, applying clips or silicone rubber rings, and blocking the tubes with chemicals or tubal inserts. The objective of this review was to compare different tubal occlusion techniques in terms of major and minor complications, failure rates (pregnancies), technical difficulties, and satisfaction levels of both women and surgeons. For the original review, databases such as MEDLINE and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) were searched. For the 2015 update, additional databases, including POPLINE, LILACS, PubMed, and CENTRAL, were searched on July 23, 2015. The PubMed related articles feature and reference lists of newly identified trials were also utilized. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared different techniques for tubal sterilization, regardless of the method of accessing the fallopian tubes or the type of anesthesia used. Data extraction for the original review was performed independently by two authors, while for the update, one author extracted the data, and another verified it. Trials were grouped based on the type of comparison, and results were reported as odds ratios (OR) or mean differences (MD) using fixed-effect methods unless significant heterogeneity was present, in which case random-effects methods were used. The review included 19 RCTs involving 13,209 women. Most studies focused on interval sterilization, while three RCTs involving 1,632 women addressed postpartum sterilization. Comparisons included tubal rings versus clips (six RCTs, 4,232 women), partial salpingectomy versus electrocoagulation (three RCTs, 2,019 women), tubal rings versus electrocoagulation (two RCTs, 599 women), partial salpingectomy versus clips (four RCTs, 3,627 women), clips versus electrocoagulation (two RCTs, 206 women), and Hulka versus Filshie clips (two RCTs, 2,326 women). No data were available from RCTs comparing clips to electrocoagulation. Failure rates one year after sterilization were low (<5 per 1,000) for all methods. No deaths were reported with any technique, and major complications related to the occlusion methods were rare. However, minor complications were more frequent with tubal rings compared to clips (Peto OR 2.15, 95% CI 1.22 to 3.78; participants = 842; studies = 2; I² = 0%; high-quality evidence). Technical failures were also more common with tubal rings (Peto OR 3.93, 95% CI 2.43 to 6.35; participants = 3,476; studies = 3; I² = 0%; high-quality evidence). Major complications were significantly higher with the modified Pomeroy technique compared to electrocoagulation (Peto OR 2.87, 95% CI 1.13 to 7.25; participants = 1,905; studies = 2; I² = 0%; low-quality evidence). Postoperative pain was also more frequent with the modified Pomeroy technique (Peto OR 3.85, 95% CI 2.91 to 5.10; participants = 1,905; studies = 2; I² = 0%; moderate-quality evidence). When comparing tubal rings to electrocoagulation, postoperative pain was significantly more common with tubal rings (OR 3.40, 95% CI 1.17 to 9.84; participants = 596; studies = 2; I² = 87%; low-quality evidence). When partial salpingectomy was compared to clips, no major complications were reported in either group (participants = 2,198; studies = 1). Minor complications were infrequent and not significantly different between the groups (Peto OR 7.39, 95% CI 0.46 to 119.01; participants = 193; studies = 1; low-quality evidence). However, technical failures were more common with clips (Peto OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.40; participants = 2,198; studies = 1; moderate-quality evidence). Operative time was shorter with clips compared to partial salpingectomy (MD 4.26 minutes, 95% CI 3.65 to 4.86; participants = 2,223; studies = 2; I² = 0%; high-quality evidence). There was limited evidence regarding the satisfaction of women or surgeons with the different techniques. No RCTs compared tubal microinserts (hysteroscopic sterilization) or chemical inserts (quinacrine) to other methods. In conclusion, tubal sterilization using partial salpingectomy, electrocoagulation, clips, or rings is a safe and effective contraceptive method. Failure rates at 12 months post-sterilization and major complications are rare with any of these techniques. However, minor complications and technical failures are more common with tubal rings compared to clips. Electrocoagulation may result in less postoperative pain than the modified Pomeroy or tubal ring methods. Further research should focus on RCTs to evaluate the effectiveness and controlled observational studies to assess adverse effects of minimally invasive sterilization methods, such as tubal inserts and quinacrine.
